en.title: The Book of De · Chapter Twenty-five · The Pouring-place
en.原文:
道者 萬物之注也 善人之保也 不善人之所寳也

美言可以市 尊行可以賀人 人之不善 何棄之有 

故立天子 置三卿 雖有拱之璧以先四馬 不善坐 而進此

古之所以貴此者何也 不謂求以得 有罪以免輿 故為天下貴
en.字龕:
### 注 *zhù* ／ 奧 *ào* — the pouring-place ／ the inner corner （校勘龕 · collation niche）

**字 Graph** ｜ 篆 ![注之篆](/book-assets/hosuke-laozi-en/zhuan/%E6%B3%A8.svg) ![奧之篆](/book-assets/hosuke-laozi-en/zhuan/%E5%A5%A7.svg)

The silk text reads 道者萬物之**注** where the Wang Bi recension reads **奧**. The *Shuowen*: 「注，灌也。從水，主聲。」 — "to pour. From 水, water, with 主 as sound": the place all waters are poured. And 「奧，宛也。室之西南隅。」 — "the southwest inner corner of the house" — the deepest corner, seat of the ancestral spirits. Two pictures of the Dao: the pool every stream pours into, or the darkest corner of the house. The commentary below rules for the silk text: pouring is flow that reaches everything; the corner is a thing stored away and hard to know — and Laozi's Dao is no occult science but the running of the self-so.
en.對校:
道者萬物之奧。
:
善人之寶，
:
不善人之所保。
:
美言可以市，尊行可以加人。
:
人之不善，何棄之有？
:
故立天子，置三公，
:
雖有拱璧以先駟馬，不如坐進此道。
:
古之所以貴此道者何？不曰以求得，有罪以免邪？故為天下貴。
:
en.疏:
杳眇曰：

道之於物，猶水之就下，百川之歸壑也。此章首句，帛書作「萬物之注」，王弼本作「萬物之奧」——注者流而普被，奧者藏而難知。奧使道為隱密之玄機，注使道為江海之流行。帛書義遠勝，老子之道非奧秘之學，乃自然之運，萬物所趨赴而莫之能禦者。今人讀王弼本而以道為秘奧，此王弼注疏之失，非經本然也。

夫道者，善人寶之，不善人亦寶之。善人視道為寶，不善之人亦知貴此道。蓋道之普覆，無間乎人之賢愚善不善。孔子論善人，言其質美而未學，「不踐跡，亦不入於室」，是其人稟賦雖善，終不能深造乎道；老子則不分彼此，一體同仁。孔子嚴其責而求之深，老子廣其容而待之恕，二家之異於此可見，而所求之終歸於一也。

「美言可以市，尊行可以賀人」，帛書乙本作「賀」，甲本與王弼同作「加」。賀者致慶，賀近道家之和；加者施惠，加近儒家之施。賀者平等，加者上下——乙本義更合老子道之平等。美言得利於市，尊行致慶於人，言行之可以致用如此，天下無可棄之人也。

「立天子，置三卿」，帛書作「三卿」，王弼作「三公」。卿者官之大者，公者爵之尊者；帛書近實，王弼近名。「拱之璧以先駟馬」，至貴之禮也；「不如坐進此道」，內之實也。拱璧駟馬可以為儀，道可以為本；天子之所以為天子，在其得道，非在其受璧。「善人之寶」之義，可與此相發。

「古之所以貴此者何也？不謂求以得，有罪以免。」得道之效：求者能得，罪者能免。非道之為功利，乃道一通則內外皆通——內通則無所求而自得，外通則有罪而自赦。所謂得一而天下正，此之謂乎！故曰為天下貴——天下之所以貴道者，非以其奇，乃以其常；非以其外，乃以其內；非以其奧，乃以其注也。
en.疏英:
Yaomiao says:

The Dao is to the ten thousand things what the downhill is to water: the hundred streams going home to the hollow. The chapter's first line: the silk text has 萬物之注, "where the ten thousand things pour"; the Wang Bi recension has 奧, "the inner corner." **注 is flow reaching everything; 奧 is a thing stored away and hard to know.** 奧 makes the Dao a hidden mystery; 注 makes it the moving water of rivers and seas. The silk text's sense is far the stronger: Laozi's Dao is no esoteric doctrine but the operation of the self-so: the place all things stream toward, which nothing can dam. Those who read Wang Bi and take the Dao for an arcanum are misled by the commentator, not by the classic.

The Dao: the good man treasures it, and the not-good man treasures it too. The good man holds the Dao as treasure; the man not good also knows to prize it. The Dao's covering is universal, indifferent to a man's worth or want of it. Confucius, speaking of the merely good man, says he "does not tread in the footprints, nor does he enter the room": well endowed, yet never going deep. Laozi draws no such line: one body, one kindness. Confucius is strict in demand and deep in requirement; Laozi is wide in embrace and forgiving in expectation: here the two houses part, and what they seek comes in the end to one.

"Fine words can be traded in the market; honored conduct can grace other men": silk manuscript B writes 賀, "to grace with congratulation"; manuscript A, like Wang Bi, writes 加, "to bestow upon." To congratulate is a courtesy between equals, near the Daoist's harmony; to bestow is a favor from above, near the Confucian's charity. Manuscript B's graph better fits the equality of Laozi's Dao. If even words can fetch a price and conduct can be offered in congratulation, then in all-under-heaven there is no discardable man.

"Enthrone the Son of Heaven, install the three ministers": the silk text says 三卿, Wang Bi 三公: minister is the greater office, duke the loftier title; the silk text stays near the practical, Wang Bi near the nominal. The jade disc borne ahead of the four-horse team is the costliest of ceremonies — and not so good as sitting still and advancing this Dao: the inward substance against the outward show. Discs and horses make a rite; the Dao makes the root. What makes the Son of Heaven the Son of Heaven is his getting of the Dao, not his receiving of jade.

"Why did the ancients prize this? Did they not say: seek, and by it you find; be guilty, and by it you are spared." The effect of getting the Dao: the seeker finds, the guilty goes free. Not that the Dao trades in profit: when the Dao runs through, inside and outside both run through: within, one finds without seeking; without, one is pardoned though guilty. Get the One, and all-under-heaven comes straight — is that not this? Hence: the prized of all-under-heaven. All-under-heaven prizes the Dao not for its strangeness but for its constancy; not for what it is outside but for what it is within; **not because it is the corner, but because it is the pouring-place.**
en.英譯:
The Dao (道) is where the ten thousand things pour (注): the safeguard (保) of the good man, and what the not-good man holds as treasure too.

Fine words can be traded in the market; honored conduct can be offered in congratulation to others (賀人). As for a man's not-being-good: what discarding could there be?

So when the Son of Heaven is enthroned and the three ministers installed: though the arm-clasped jade disc go ahead of the four-horse team, that is not so good as sitting where you are and advancing this Dao.

Why did the ancients prize this? Did they not say: seek, and by it you find; be guilty, and by it you are spared? Therefore it is the prized of all-under-heaven.
